Figure 4-22. Flight maneuvers that display altitude changes on an uncompensated variometer. Electric-powered variometers offer several advantages over the non-electric variety. These advantages include more rapid response rates and separate audible signals for climb and descent. Some electric variometers use special sensors. As air flows into or out of the reference chamber, it cools sensors in a circuit and alters the electrical resistance measured by the system. The resulting change in resistance corresponds to the rate of climb or descent. The system displays that information on the variometer. Many electric variometers provide audible tones, or beeps, that indicate the rate of climb or rate of descent of the glider. Pilots using an audio variometer can listen for the rate of climb or descent, which allows more time to focus attention outside the aircraft. [Figure 4-23] 4-14
